# Relative Humidity, Temperature, and Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy: Findings from the Project Viva Cohort

**Authors:** Christina M. Howe; Brent A. Coull; Stefania Papatheodorou; Heike Luttmann-Gibson; Sheryl L. Rifas-Shiman; Ander Wilson; Itai Kloog; Qian Di; Antonella Zanobetti; Petros Koutrakis; Joel D. Schwartz; Emily Oken; Diane R. Gold

**Affiliations:** 1:Department of Biostatistics, Harvard School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 2:Department of Environmental Health, Harvard School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 3:Division of Chronic Disease Research Across the Lifecourse, Department of Population Medicine, Harvard Medical School and Harvard Pilgrim Health Care Institute, Boston, MA, USA. | 4:Department of Statistics, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA | 5:Department of Environmental Medicine and Public Health at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, USA; Department of Geography at Ben Gurion University of the Negev, Beersheba Israel | 6:Vanke School of Public Health, Tsinghua University, Beijing, China | 7:Department of Nutrition, Harvard T H Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA. | 8:Channing Laboratory, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, USA

## Abstract

Preeclampsia is a multi-system hypertensive disorder of pregnancy that is a leading cause of maternal and fetal morbidity and mortality. Prior studies disagree on the cause and even the presence of seasonal patterns in its incidence. Using unsuitable time windows for seasonal exposures can bias model results, potentially explaining these inconsistencies.

We aimed to investigate humidity and temperature as possible causes for seasonal trends in preeclampsia in Project Viva, a prebirth cohort in Boston, Massachusetts, considering only exposure windows that precede disease onset.

Using the Parameter-elevation Relationships on Independent Slopes Model (PRISM) Climate Dataset, we estimated daily residential temperature and relative humidity (RH) exposures during pregnancy. Our primary multinomial regression adjusted for person-level covariates and season. Secondary analyses included distributed lag models (DLMs) and adjusted for ambient air pollutants including fine particulates (PM2.5). We used Generalized Additive Mixed Models (GAMMs) for systolic blood pressure (SBP) trajectories across hypertensive disorder statuses to confirm exposure timing.

While preeclampsia is typically diagnosed late in pregnancy, GAMM-fitted SBP trajectories for preeclamptic and non-preeclamptic women began to diverge at around 20 weeks’ gestation, confirming the need to only consider early exposures. In the primary analysis with 1776 women, RH in the early second trimester, weeks 14–20, was associated with significantly higher odds of preeclampsia (OR per IQR increase: 1.81, 95% CI: 1.10, 2.97). The DLM corroborated this window, finding a positive association from weeks 12–20. There were no other significant associations between RH or temperature and preeclampsia or gestational hypertension in any other time period.

The association between preeclampsia and RH in the early second trimester was robust to model choice, suggesting that RH may contribute to seasonal trends in preeclampsia exposure timing differences.

## INTRODUCTION:

Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, characterized by elevated blood pressure occurring after 20 weeks’ gestation, include both gestational hypertension and the more severe preeclampsia, which also involves proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction. Preeclampsia is a leading cause of maternal-fetal morbidity and mortality (Duly 2009; Lain 2002) and is associated with a 5-fold increase in infant mortality (Mendola et al. 2015) and a 2- to 4-fold increased future maternal risk of stroke, coronary heart disease, heart failure, and cardiovascular disease mortality (Bellamy et al. 2007). Approximately 5–7% of pregnancies are affected by preeclampsia, and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy were the sixth leading cause of maternal deaths in the US from 2017–2019 (CDC 2020). Most of the known risk factors for preeclampsia, including nulliparity, Black race, extremes of age, renal disease, and previous hypertension or preeclampsia are patient-specific (Bartsch et al. 2016; Giannakou et al. 2018). However, previous studies have also demonstrated seasonal patterns in the incidence of preeclampsia, which may be due to seasonal variations of temperature and humidity. However, the cause and even the existence of these seasonal patterns is still a matter of debate, with other previous research suggesting associations between preeclampsia and each of cool weather, warm weather, dry weather, damp weather, sunlight hours in the month of delivery, and low barometric pressure, among other factors (Liao et al. 2023; Melo et al. 2014; Tan et al. 1988; Tran et al. 2015). Other studies have found no association between hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and season or climatic factors (Magann et al. 1995; Subramaniam 2007).

Of studies involving climate and preeclampsia, few have limited their exposure assessment to time windows preceding disease onset and, to our knowledge, none has used a distributed lag model, a method that can facilitate identification of the critical window of exposure in a data-driven way. In this study, we aimed to evaluate the associations of temperature and relative humidity with gestational hypertension and preeclampsia using data from the Project Viva cohort in Boston, Massachusetts.

## METHODS:

For this analysis, study subjects were participants in Project Viva, a Boston-area prospective observational cohort of 2,128 pregnancies resulting in a live singleton birth. Women were recruited during their first prenatal visit to one of eight urban and suburban obstetrical offices with Atrius Harvard Vanguard Medical Associates from 1999 to 2002. The details of this cohort are described elsewhere (Oken et al. 2014). All participating mothers provided informed consent and institutional review boards of participating institutions approved the study.

### Exposure Assessment:

We a priori considered four possible exposure windows for analysis, all occurring before diagnosis of a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy: the first trimester (weeks 0 through 13 and 6 days, the halved first trimesters (weeks 0 through 6 and 6 days and weeks 7 through 13 and 6 days), and the part of the second trimester preceding 20 weeks, after which preeclampsia can be diagnosed (weeks 14 through 19 and 6 days). We will hereafter refer to the latter time period as the first half of the second trimester. As a comparison, we also included the entirety of the second trimester and the part of the second trimester after 20 weeks’ gestation, hereafter referred to as the second half of the second trimester, though exposures after 20 weeks should not be considered as causal since they occur after possible disease onset.

We used the 800-meter resolution PRISM Spatial Climate Dataset for the Conterminous United States to extract daily mean temperature and mean relative humidity estimates for cohort maternal address locations during pregnancy (PRISM 2021). The PRISM procedure is regarded as one of the most reliable spatiotemporal models for small-scale climate data and has previously been shown to be useful in environmental epidemiology studies (Spangler et al. 2019). Relative humidity is a percentage of water vapor present in the air compared to the total possible amount of water vapor at the current temperature. These daily exposures were then matched with day of pregnancy, as initially measured by the date of the last menstrual period and then updated with ultrasound. These daily exposures were averaged over the six exposure windows and standardized by interquartile range within that exposure window.

Air pollution exposure was included as a possible confounder or mediator in sensitivity analyses, again averaged over the six exposure windows (first trimester, second trimester, and the first and second half of each of the first and second trimester). Again, the only exposure periods that could be considered to be causal are those occurring prior to 20 weeks of pregnancy, so the first trimester and its halves and the first half of the second trimester. We estimated daily ambient levels of multiple pollutants at the maternal residence throughout pregnancy via spatiotemporal models validated to have good predictive performance in the study region. Briefly, fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentration levels were estimated across the Northeastern United States at a 1×1 km spatial resolution using a hybrid satellite-based model incorporating daily satellite remote sensing data, monitored concentrations, meteorological variables, and land use regression variables (Kloog et al. 2014). Particulate components elemental carbon, organic carbon, and nitrate concentration levels were also estimated across the Northeastern United States at a 1×1 km spatial resolution using a hybrid prediction model that integrated output from a chemical transport model, ground monitoring data, meteorological variables, land-use terms, and spatiotemporal lagged terms (Di et al. 2016). Both sets of estimates are available on a daily basis only starting in 2000, so earlier pregnancies in the cohort do not have these exposures. Daily predictions accounting for residential moves were generated for each day during pregnancy where available.

### Outcome Assessment:

Blood pressure measurements were taken during outpatient clinical visits. To diagnose hypertensive disorder status, outpatient charts were reviewed for blood pressure and results of urine protein screening. When women had a diagnosis or discharge code indicating preeclampsia or gestational hypertension and did not meet criteria for preeclampsia or gestational hypertension based on outpatient charts, inpatient hospital charts were also reviewed. We classified a woman as having chronic hypertension if she was taking antihypertensive medication pre-pregnancy or if she had two elevated clinically measured blood pressure values before 20 weeks of gestation (systolic (SBP) >140 mm Hg or diastolic (DBP) >90 mm Hg) and did not subsequently develop preeclampsia. We defined preeclampsia and gestational hypertension according to the contemporaneous recommendations of the National High Blood Pressure Education Program (“Report of the National High Blood Pressure” 2000). We categorized a woman as having preeclampsia if she had chronic hypertension and developed proteinuria (dipstick value of 1+ on two or more occasions or ≥2+ once) > 4 hours but ≤ 7 days apart after 20 weeks of gestation, or if she did not have chronic hypertension but developed elevated blood pressure and proteinuria after 20 weeks gestation. We categorized a woman as having gestational hypertension if she did not have chronic hypertension and developed elevated blood pressure on at least two separate occasions after 20 weeks of pregnancy without developing proteinuria. Of the 2,128 pregnancies, we excluded from the primary analyses 28 (1.3%) of subsequent pregnancies for women who were enrolled twice, 31 (1.5%) of the remaining who did not have reviewable medical records, and 27 (1.3%) who had chronic hypertension without developing preeclampsia. Of the remaining 2,042 pregnancies (96.0%) available for this study, 135 (6.6%) had gestational hypertension, 74 (3.6%) had preeclampsia, and 1,833 (89.8%) did not meet the criteria for any hypertensive disorder.

### Covariate Assessment:

Study visits were performed after the mothers’ prenatal clinical appointments at study enrollment (median 10.4 weeks of gestation) and mid-pregnancy (26–28 weeks). Using a combination of interviews and questionnaires, information was collected on participants’ age at enrollment, race/ethnicity, education level, household income, and parity. Pre-pregnancy body mass index (BMI, kg/m2) was calculated from self-reported height and pre-pregnancy weight. Participants’ classification of glucose tolerance status was based on routine glucose screening at the end of the second trimester (median: 28.1 weeks), which is after preeclampsia onset.

### Statistical Analyses:

Chi-squared tests were used to determine associations of season of a blinded early pregnancy date with hypertensive disorder status, education level (defined as college graduate or not a college graduate), income level (defined as greater than $70,000/year or not), having a female fetus, and parity. Fisher’s exact tests with simulated p-values were used for the associations with race and smoking status. One-way ANOVA tests were used to determine the associations of hypertensive disorder status with BMI and age.

To inspect differences in blood pressure trajectories among women with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and those without, we used a generalized additive mixed model (GAMM) to estimate the trajectories of SBP and DBP as a smooth function of gestational age, stratified by hypertensive disorder status. GAMM models estimate these trajectories by combining the flexible, data-driven smoothing approach from Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) and the random effects from mixed models to account for repeated measures (Wood 2017).

To determine the associations of relative humidity and temperature with hypertensive disorder status, we used multinomial logistic regression to estimate associations of each of temperature and relative humidity exposures over each of the six exposure time periods (first trimester, second trimester, and the first and second half of each of the first and second trimester) with the outcome categories (no hypertensive disease, gestational hypertension, and preeclampsia).

The primary regression models were adjusted for pre-pregnancy BMI, parity (categorized into nulliparous vs. parous), fetal sex, maternal age at enrollment, education level, household income level, and race/ethnicity. We adjusted for any lingering seasonal confounding by including the season of, and sine and cosine of a blinded early pregnancy date in our models. Project Viva has a low number of smokers so it was not statistically appropriate to include smoking status in the primary model for stability of the effect estimates. Although gestational diabetes and preeclampsia are often comorbid conditions, the hormonal contributors to insulin resistance in gestational diabetes typically occur after preeclampsia onset, so again this was not an appropriate covariate to include within the primary model as its inclusion could introduce bias. Income is the variable with highest missingness at 11.8%, with all other variables having missingness under 1%. As income is a very important confounder for environmental exposures and preeclampsia and we assume that it is missing at random (MAR), we performed complete case analysis, leaving 1,776 women available for the primary model.

Several sensitivity analyses were performed as follows: including the n = 27 women with chronic hypertension as an additional outcome in the multinomial regression; removing temperature from the primary model; including a non-linear (GAM) association of relative humidity and temperature to account for dose-dependent effects; including an interaction term between temperature and relative humidity; including smoking status as an additional covariate; including first SBP measurement as an additional covariate that serves as a proxy for pre-pregnancy SBP; including residence distance from a major road and residential traffic as confounders; including neighborhood-level income and educational attainment as confounders; including non-linear adjustment (GAM) for maternal age; including employment outside of the home as a covariate to account for exposure assessment error; and excluding women with Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes. Finally, the primary multinomial regression model was re-run adding the spatiotemporally estimated air pollutants (PM2.5, elemental carbon, organic carbon, nitrate, and ozone) one-at-a-time. These spatiotemporal estimates have the advantage that they likely reduce exposure error associated with a single central-site monitor but are only available starting in 2000, reducing the sample size for these analyses. Because the availability of exposure data was due to this timing and not maternal characteristics, complete case analysis was performed.

Although easy to interpret clinically, trimesters and halves of trimesters have limited biological underpinning. Therefore, we applied distributed lag logistic regression models (DLMs) to data from women with preeclampsia and those without a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy to estimate the critical window for this outcome more flexibly. For these analyses, women with chronic hypertension and gestational hypertension were excluded. Containing a coefficient for exposure on each individual day during the first 22 weeks of pregnancy, distributed lag models used a natural cubic spline with 5 degrees of freedom to impose structure on the coefficient estimates as a function of exposure time. We chose to include an additional 3 weeks of exposure to reduce edge effects and 5 degrees of freedom to balance flexibility and overfitting. We ran models containing a distributed lag for relative humidity only, for temperature only, and for both, while keeping all other covariates from the primary model unchanged. The covariates were the same as in the primary model. We also performed a sensitivity analysis using 7 degrees of freedom for the natural cubic spline.

These multinomial analyses were performed using VGAM package version 1.1–5 in R version 4.0.4. The GAMM SBP trajectories were performed using the mgcv package version 1.8–34. The DLM analyses were performed with an edited version of the Regimes package to allow for multiple exposures. Code is available upon request.

## RESULTS:

Hypothesis testing showed significant associations of hypertensive disorder status with race, parity, education level, and BMI (Table 1). The unadjusted odds ratio for preeclampsia comparing individuals exposed to mean relative humidity above the 75th percentile during weeks 14–20 versus those below the 75th percentile during weeks 14–20 was 1.59 (95% CI: (0.97, 2.61)) (Table 2).

### Blood Pressure Trends:

The generalized additive mixed model (GAMM) smoothing of systolic blood pressure as a function of gestation duration, stratified by hypertensive disorder status, shows distinct differences in both initial systolic blood pressure and the shape of the blood pressure trajectory among these groups of women (Figure 1). In women without a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy, the initial systolic blood pressure (SBP) is lower and the characteristic decrease in SBP occurred on average from weeks 0 to 20 with the characteristic increase beginning around week 32. In women with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, the decrease in the first trimester was still present, but the increase began at around 20 weeks of gestation, occurring slightly earlier in women with preeclampsia as opposed to gestational hypertension. This shows that it is inappropriate to use exposure windows after 20 weeks of gestation in studies involving hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and also supports using the clinical 20-week cutoff for disease diagnosis. We performed a sensitivity analysis using the first SBP measurement as a proxy for pre-pregnancy blood pressure to reflect the difference in starting points for these trajectories.

### Exposure:

Relative humidity and mean temperature over the study period as estimated by the PRISM model ranged from 7.4 to 100% and −17.1 to 30.9 degrees Celsius, respectively. In Boston, daily relative humidity and temperature, recorded during the first half of the second trimester, were not strongly correlated, with a Spearman correlation of 0.16 for daily measurements during the first half of the second trimester. The mean temperature and the mean relative humidity averaged over this entire time-period are more highly correlated, with a Spearman correlation of 0.39.

### Relative Humidity and Odds of Preeclampsia:

Of the time periods and exposures considered in our multinomial regression, only the association between mean relative humidity in the first half of the second trimester and preeclampsia was significant (OR per IQR increase = 1.81, 95% CI: 1.10, 2.97 (Figure 2)). The association between relative humidity and preeclampsia was not statistically significant in any other time period. The association between temperature and preeclampsia was not statistically significant in any time period; and the associations between each of temperature and relative humidity with gestational hypertension were not statistically significant in any time period (Supplemental Figure 1).

### Sensitivity Analyses:

Sensitivity analyses show the robustness of these estimates to model selection. The point estimate OR per IQR increase in RH in the first half of the second trimester ranged from 1.82 to 2.04 when the ambient air pollutants PM2.5, elemental carbon, nitrate, and ozone were included in the model one-at-a-time. All other sensitivity analyses had point estimate ORs that ranged from 1.75 to 1.91 per IQR of RH in this time period. These analyses included: the inclusion of the n = 27 women with chronic hypertension as an additional outcome, no temperature variable in the model, a non-linear effect of relative humidity using an additive model (which had a p-value of 0.08 for the non-linear component), including smoking status as a covariate, including employment status as a covariate, including the first systolic blood pressure measurement as a covariate, removing women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes (n = 16), allowing a non-linear effect of maternal age using an additive model (p-value for non-linear component = 0.15), including residence distance from a major road and a residential traffic level as confounders, and including neighborhood-level poverty and education as confounders. When an interaction term between temperature and relative humidity was added to the main model, the p-value for this interaction term was non-significant (p-value = 0.24).

### Distributed Lag Model:

The data-driven distributed lag model (DLM) corroborates the time window corresponding to the first half of the second trimester (Figure 3). There is a positive association between daily relative humidity and preeclampsia from 12 weeks and 0 days through 20 weeks and 0 days, and the 95% pointwise confidence interval does not contain the null from 14 weeks and 3 days through 18 weeks and 3 days. The DLMs for gestational hypertension as the outcome and for temperature as the exposure were null throughout (Supplemental Figures 2-4). The DLM with 7 degrees of freedom rather than 5 showed a very similar result, with a positive association between relative humidity and preeclampsia from 12 weeks and 4 days through 19 weeks and 5 days (Supplemental Figure 5).

## Discussion:

The three very different modeling approaches of a series of unadjusted odds ratios (Table 2), a series of multinomial regressions (Figure 2), and a distributed lag model (Figure 3) all show a strong positive association between relative humidity exposure in the first half of the second trimester and preeclampsia risk. Depending on the analysis, we observed 79% to 104% increased odds of preeclampsia per IQR increase in mean relative humidity exposure during the first half of the second trimester of pregnancy (14 weeks and 0 days through 19 weeks and 6 days), with the primary model that adjusted for temperature, early pregnancy date and season, and maternal characteristics showing 81% increased odds. A distributed lag model indicated a positive association between preeclampsia and relative humidity from 12 weeks to 20 weeks, confirming the critical window for this exposure as the first half of the second trimester. No statistically significant association was found between preeclampsia and temperature or early pregnancy season, and no statistically significant association was found between gestational hypertension and relative humidity, temperature, or early pregnancy season. The distributed lag models were also null for these exposures and outcomes.

Previous studies have considered the association between relative humidity, season, and preeclampsia. For a few examples, a retrospective cohort study from Immink et al (2008) analyzed 11,585 pregnancies in South Africa and observed that pregnant women admitted to the hospital in winter had higher rates of preeclampsia. Weinberg et al (2017) examined over 13,000 cases of preeclampsia from the Medical Birth Registry in Norway from 1999 to 2009 and found that there was a higher risk of preeclampsia in spring conceptions. As winter months in South Africa are the warm season and spring conceptions mean late summer second trimester, these seemingly contradictory results may actually point to a related phenomenon, which is that those experiencing the second half of pregnancy in warmer, more humid months are at higher risk of developing preeclampsia. A recent systematic review of twenty articles and meta-analysis of eleven showed increased odds of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy among women who delivered in winter (Liao et al. 2023). In another seemingly contradictory study using 2,495,383 births from Korea National Health Insurance claims data, the authors found a statistically significant negative association between mean monthly relative humidity and monthly preeclampsia prevalence, in contrast to our positive association (Cho et al. 2017). However, by using exposures in late pregnancy, such as the month of diagnosis or delivery as is typical in prevalence-based studies, one can obtain biased and even opposite-sign effect estimates when the exposure exhibits seasonal trends and the true association occurs in an earlier trimester (Wilson et al. 2017). As the time window in our study occurs approximately 5 months before delivery and South Korea has a wet season and a dry season, it is plausible that their study would actually confirm our results if the same methods were applied. Magann et al. (1995) reported no seasonal variation in preeclampsia prevalence in Mississippi, where temperature varies throughout the year and relative humidity is consistently high. They also note the high preeclampsia prevalence of 8.3%, though this could be due to many other factors including maternal characteristics and selection bias from delivering at a tertiary medical center. Many other studies have considered the seasonal trends in preeclampsia but typically have considered exposures at the time of delivery, diagnosis, or conception rather than as time-varying throughout the pregnancy. Auger et al. (2017) argue that observed seasonality in preeclampsia prevalence is due to bias from considering exposures in the month of delivery due to shorter gestation in preeclampsia, though this is not relevant to our prospective study design. We argue that bias from using exposures in the month of delivery is not only due to differences in gestation time but also to using exposures that occur after disease process onset.

The potential pathophysiological mechanism in the association between relative humidity and preeclampsia is unclear. Increased relative humidity may lead to decreased perspiration and changes in sweat composition and thus could increase intravascular volume and systolic blood pressure in susceptible women (Baker 2019; Kondo et al. 2001). Supporting this theory, we observed that women with preeclampsia had, on average, a slightly smaller decrease in blood pressure through the first 20 weeks of pregnancy than women without a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy, as seen in Figure 1. There is also some evidence of humidity increasing the risk of cardiovascular diseases including thrombosis (Zeng et al. 2017). It is also possible that relative humidity is tightly correlated with other climatic exposures that were unmeasured in this study such as apparent temperature or with changes in circadian rhythm, diet, physical activity, respiratory infection incidence, or vitamin D levels and consequently calcium metabolism (Mirzakhani et al. 2016; Palacios et al. 2019).

The strengths of this study include careful consideration of the exposure timing in relation to the onset of preeclampsia, the thorough data collection methods available through Project Viva, and the numerous sensitivity analyses which showed robustness of these results to the choice of model. Weaknesses include the observational nature of the study, generalizability to geographic regions outside of Boston and to other patient populations, and the possibility of unmeasured confounding. Due to sample size, we were not able to examine the association between early (<34 weeks) and late (>34 weeks) onset preeclampsia, which probably have different pathophysiology and contribute unequally to adverse pregnancy outcomes.

## Conclusions

Based on the current data, relative humidity may play a significant role in the development of preeclampsia. Given that exposure to environmental risk factors is modifiable, this finding is of public health importance. Future studies with broader geographical regions and larger, more representative cohorts that use distributed lag models or other methods to identify windows of susceptibility are needed to disentangle the role of relative humidity and other environmental exposures in the development of preeclampsia.
